changes.current:
Two consequences carried into the text. The GO Opus-selected run regresses
−10.3 points on re-scoring because every seed sits at the extreme of a noisy
distribution, and it is range-restricted — it cannot contain the low band
where New Brunswick found most of its successes, so its zero successes are

were scanned. It is also every Government Orders positive we hold, so it is an
exploratory replication rather than an independent rate estimate.

changes.locus: Appendix B — “The elevenfold spread.”
changes.current:
**The elevenfold spread.** Earlier versions stated the cross-chamber
spread as the raw range of the twenty per-chamber rates, 1.8% to 19.8% —
elevenfold. Superseded by the random-effects treatment in §4.2: the
extremes of twenty noisy estimates are extreme partly by sampling luck, so
a raw max/min ratio overstates true separation. Under empirical-Bayes
shrinkage (logit τ = 0.56, I² = 0.78) the range is 4.3% to 18.3% —
better than fourfold — which is the figure the paper now
reports.[^rshrink]
changes.proposed:
**The elevenfold spread.** Earlier versions described the raw range of
the twenty per-chamber rates, 1.8% to 19.8%, as an elevenfold spread. That
statement is superseded by the random-effects treatment in §4.2. Because
the extremes of twenty noisy estimates partly reflect sampling luck, the
raw maximum-to-minimum ratio overstates the underlying separation. After
empirical-Bayes shrinkage (logit τ = 0.56, I² = 0.78), the range is 4.3% to
18.3% — more than fourfold — which is the figure the paper now
reports.[^rshrink]
changes.rationale: This states the statistical reason for retiring the old figure in a cleaner sequence and replaces the awkward “better than fourfold” with the precise interpretation, without changing any estimate.

changes.locus: Appendix C, item 1 — “The substance channel.”
changes.current:
1. **The substance channel.** §4 measures *register*. Whether machine
   assistance changes what legislators argue, which evidence they cite, and
   which framings they reach for is unmeasured, and the Kobak instrument cannot
   answer it — its style/content split is PubMed's content, not a legislature's,
   and does not transfer. The materials for a domain-native version already
   exist: the base-versus-instruct generation that produced §4.8's +0.387 yields
   an empirically derived list of what post-training adds *to legislative text
   specifically*. Split that list into register-like and substance-like by an
   independent rule and run both through the frozen protocol as separate arms,
   giving "did the register shift" and "did the substance shift" as two
   measurements instead of one. Estimated at a few hours. This is the single
   most valuable unrun item, and it is also a limit on the present study rather
   than merely an extension (§6).
changes.proposed:
1. **The substance channel.** §4 measures *register*, not whether machine
   assistance changes what legislators argue, which evidence they cite, or
   which framings they reach for. The Kobak instrument cannot answer that
   question: its style/content split captures PubMed's content and does not
   transfer to a legislature. A domain-native test can be built from materials
   already in hand. The base-versus-instruct generation that produced §4.8's
   +0.387 yields an empirical list of what post-training adds to legislative
   text specifically. Divide that list into register-like and substance-like
   features by an independent rule, then run both as separate arms through the
   frozen protocol. The result would be two measurements — “did the register
   shift?” and “did the substance shift?” — instead of one. Estimated at a few
   hours, this is the most valuable unrun item and a limit on the present study,
   not merely an extension (§6).

changes.locus: Appendix C, item 17 — "Members read what staff write, so a 70-year-old member"
changes.current: 17. **Staff age as the exposure measure.** Members read what staff write, so a 70-year-old member with 24-year-old staff has young exposure — which is why the member-age design is not the right one. Legislative staff are young and short-tenured, so office exposure tracks the cohort entering staff work, and that cohort turned computer-native in the mid-2000s, where the UK curve starts climbing. Data is thin but two routes exist: Legistorm's US congressional staff records (paid) and House Statements of Disbursements (names, salaries, tenure and salary as seniority proxies). Neither has been pursued.

changes.locus: Appendix C, item 4 — “The anti-correlation of gut judgment”
changes.current:
4. **The anti-correlation of gut judgment, measured properly.** §7.2's
   sharpest claim — that register-based human judgment of authorship is
   anti-correlated with the truth on adversarial text, flagging real humans
   more than optimised machine rewrites — currently rests on one unblinded,
   lineage-correlated judge (the DQI grader shares a family with the search's
   own Opus proxy) over 35 texts, where the paired effect is directional but
   not significant (−4 points, t = −1.15). The confirmatory design is cheap
   and pre-registerable: recruit human raters (or at minimum a
   non-Claude-family model, so the judge is independent of the optimisation
   target), give them a balanced blind mix of genuine floor speech, ordinary
   machine drafts, and detector-optimised rewrites, and record whether the
   false-positive rate on real humans exceeds the miss rate on optimised text.
   If it does, "detection cannot underwrite an accusation" strengthens from a
   statement about detectors to a statement about human judgment itself, with
   a measured false-accusation rate attached — the number a disclosure-norm
   policy would actually need.
changes.proposed:
4. **The anti-correlation of gut judgment, measured properly.** §7.2's
   sharpest claim is that register-based authorship judgment becomes
   anti-correlated with truth on adversarial text, flagging genuine human speech
   more often than optimised machine rewrites. The present evidence is one
   unblinded, lineage-correlated judge over 35 texts: the DQI grader shares a
   model family with the search's Opus proxy, and the paired effect is
   directional but not significant (−4 points, t = −1.15). A confirmatory test
   is cheap and pre-registerable. Recruit human raters — or, at minimum, use a
   non-Claude-family model independent of the optimisation target — and give
   them a balanced, blind mixture of genuine floor speech, ordinary machine
   drafts, and detector-optimised rewrites. Then test whether the false-positive
   rate on genuine human speech exceeds the miss rate on optimised text. If it
   does, “detection cannot underwrite an accusation” extends from detectors to
   human judgment, with the measured false-accusation rate that a disclosure
   policy would need.
